'''Anna Merz''' ({{Nee}} Hepburn; 17 November 1931 – 4 April 2013) was an English conservationist who established the Ngare Sergoi Rhino Sanctuary (now the [[Lewa Wildlife Conservancy]]) in 1983. She postponed her retirement in Kenya in 1976 to take up the task of saving black rhinoceroses from poachers wanting to slaughter them for their horns. In 1990, Merz was named to the [[Global 500 Roll of Honour]] by the [[United Nations Environment Programme]]. Following her death, a female rhinoceros calf was named Anna after her and two fictional books about Merz and a rhinoceros named Samia were published in the late 2010s.

==Early life==
On 17 November 1931, Florence Ann Hepburn was born in [[Radlett]], [[Hertfordshire]], England,<ref name=EBEntry>{{cite encyclopedia|last=Schreiber|first=Barbara A.|title=Anna Merz; British conservationist|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Anna-Merz|encyclopedia=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]|accessdate=22 December 2020|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150912053727/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Anna-Merz|archivedate=12 September 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> close to London,<ref name="DTObit" /> to a [[Chancery Court of York|Chancery Court]] barrister who went on to become a [[High Court of Justice|High Court]] judge.<ref name=BBCSWWMerz>{{cite web|title=WW2 People's War: Anna Merz|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/history/ww2peopleswar/user/89/u1933389.shtml|publisher=BBC|accessdate=22 December 2020|archive-date=22 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204700/https://www.bbc.co.uk/history/ww2peopleswar/user/89/u1933389.shtml|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="DTObit">{{cite news|title=Anna Merz|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/10082966/Anna-Merz.html|work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|date=27 May 2013|accessdate=22 December 2020|archive-date=22 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204700/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/10082966/Anna-Merz.html|url-status=live}}</ref> As a child,<ref name="NYTimesObit">{{cite news|last=Martin|first=Douglas|date=22 April 2013|title=Anna Merz, Rhino Guardian and Champion, Dies at 81|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/22/world/africa/anna-merz-protector-of-black-rhinos-dies-at-81.html|accessdate=22 December 2020|archive-date=22 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204700/https://www.nytimes.com/2013/04/22/world/africa/anna-merz-protector-of-black-rhinos-dies-at-81.html|url-status=live}}</ref> she relocated between London and Cornwall during the [[World War II|Second World War]].<ref name="TimesObit">{{cite news|title=Anna Merz|url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/A326290821/GPS?u=wikipedia&sid=GPS&xid=4e938b81|work=[[The Times]]|date=15 April 2013|accessdate=22 December 2020|via=Gale Academic OneFile|url-access=subscription|archive-date=22 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204702/https://go.gale.com/ps/i.do?p=GPS&u=wikipedia&id=GALE%7CA326290821&v=2.1&it=r&sid=GPS&asid=4e938b81|url-status=live}}</ref> Merz was sent to a boarding school in [[Dorset]] with a farm and then to [[St Margaret's School, Bushey|St Margaret's]] in [[Bushey]]. She resented St Margaret's and its underground [[air raid shelter]]s;<ref name="BBCSWWMerz" /> aged nine, her life was saved by someone she did not know when a German fighter plane attacked while she was on a beach.<ref name="NYTimesObit" /> Merz studied economics and politics at the [[University of Nottingham]] before attending [[Lincoln's Inn]] to read for the bar.<ref name="BBCSWWMerz" /><ref name="RRCObit">{{cite web|title=Anna Merz Dies at the age of 81|url=http://www.rhinoresourcecenter.com/pdf_files/138/1380093761.pdf|publisher=Rhino Resource Center|accessdate=22 December 2020|archive-date=22 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204659/http://www.rhinoresourcecenter.com/pdf_files/138/1380093761.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Career==
She travelled extensively around the world.<ref name="EBEntry" /> In 1958, Merz went to [[Ghana]], where she operated a light industrial workshop as well as training and riding ponies and was honorary warden for the Ghanaian Game Department and National Park. She went to survey sites for wildlife reserves for the Ghanaian Game Department and National Park and was the manager of an animal orphanage.<ref name="DTObit" /> Merz went on exhibitions of Northern Kenya, [[Sahara|the Sahara]] to seek suitable areas for reserves and [[Uganda]].<ref name="NYTimesObit" /><ref name="TimesObit" />

In 1976, she postponed her retirement to take up the job of saving black rhinoceroses from poachers wanting to slaughter them for their horns to deal with Chinese and South East Asian demand from herbalists for herbicidal medicine and for Arabs to carve horns into dagger dangles at a vast rate.<ref name="EBEntry" /><ref name="DTObit" /><ref name="NYTimesObit" /> With a family inheritance of $750,000,<ref name="DTObit" /> Merz set up the Ngare Sergoi Rhino Sanctuary in 1983 from a lease of {{Convert|5,000|acres||abbr=on}} of land from David Craig and his wife Delia Craig.<ref name="DTObit" /><ref name="RRCObit" /> She and the Craigs employed bush pilots, game-trackers and veterinarians to gather each of the wild rhinos in Northern Kenya to be bred and be kept safe.<ref name="DTObit" /> They also erected {{Convert|42|mi|km|abbr=on}} of {{Convert|8|ft|in|abbr=on}}-high 5,000 volt [[Electric fence|electric fencing]] to discourage potential poachers,<ref name="AnimalsJanFeb97">{{cite journal|last=Braun|first=Elisabeth|date=January–February 1997|title=Walking with rhinos: the story of Anna Merz|url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/A19065059/GPS?u=wikipedia&sid=GPS&xid=2ce80299|journal=Animals|volume=130|issue=1|page=8+|url-access=subscription|via=Gale General OneFile}}</ref> recruited spies for information of poachers and purchased a plane for surveillance.<ref name="NYTimesObit" /> Merz carried a gun and knife for protection.<ref name="NYTimesObit" /> She and the Craigs hoped protecting the habitat, working with the community and providing the rhinos heavy security would enable them to breed enough so that they could repopulate Northern Kenya and the trio were give consent from the government.<ref name="TimesObit" />

One rhinoceros Merz was particularly fond of was an orphaned black rhinoceros named Samia that lived from 15 February 1985 to 21 November 1995.<ref name="DTObit" /><ref name="AnimalsJanFeb97" /> She adopted Samia as a baby and continued to rear her until it was six years old but Samia brought her calf to visit Merz daily.<ref name="DTObit" /><ref name="RRCObit" /> Merz was named to the [[Global 500 Roll of Honour]] by the [[United Nations Environment Programme]] in 1990.<ref name="NYTimesObit" /> Throughout the 1990s, she expanded the sanctuary to {{Convert|62,000|acres||abbr=on}} and renamed it the [[Lewa Wildlife Conservancy]] in 1995.<ref name="NYTimesObit" /> Merz recruited local residents, for whom she built medical clinics and schools, and made the sanctuary open to tourists.<ref name="EBEntry" /> She retired from Lewa soon after and moved to South Africa.<ref name="TimesObit" /><ref name="RRCObit" />

Merz became increasingly vocal in the rhinoceros movement and was a member of the [[San Diego Zoo]]'s save-the-rhino initiative.<ref name="LATimes1992">{{cite news|last=Granberry|first=Michael|date=13 December 1992|title=Rhinos' Twilight Hour Grows Dim : Kenyan Activist, San Diego Zoo Fight to Preserve Endangered Beast|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-12-13-me-3925-story.html|accessdate=22 December 2020}}</ref> She served on the board of both the [[International Rhino Foundation]] and the IUCN Asian Rhino Specialist Group.<ref name="BBCSWWMerz" /><ref name="TimesObit" /> Merz agreed to be a patron of the Sebakwe Black Rhino Trust.<ref name="RRCObit" /> She went on lecture tours across the United States,<ref name="BBCSWWMerz" /> and authored works to raise awareness and funding about the rhinoceros.<ref name="TimesObit" /> Merz wrote an account of her career with rhinoceros called ''Rhino: At the Brink of Extinction'' and described her formative life in England and work with the Ghanaian Game Department in the book ''Golden Dunes and Desert Mountains''.<ref name="DTObit" />

==Personal life==

Merz disliked conducting public speeches to large groups of people because she preferred animals to humans.<ref name="LATimes1992" /> She was initially married to the Swiss industrial workshop owner Ernest Kuhn until their divorce in 1969. Her second marriage to Karl Merz lasted until his death in 1988.<ref name="DTObit" /><ref name="TimesObit" /> On 4 April 2013, Merz died in hospital in Melkrivier, South Africa.<ref name="EBEntry" /><ref name="APObit">{{cite news|last=Torchia|first=Christopher|title=Rhino conservationist dies in South Africa|url=https://apnews.com/article/6174058a61e245f2b6d869073f84f0b5|agency=[[Associated Press]]|date=22 April 2013|accessdate=22 December 2020|archive-date=22 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204702/https://apnews.com/article/6174058a61e245f2b6d869073f84f0b5|url-status=live}}</ref> A memorial service was held for her at the Lewa Wildlife Conservancy on 12 May 2013.<ref name="APObit" />

==Legacy==

According to Barbara A. Schreiber in Merz's entry in ''[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]'', the conservationist "was a leading advocate for the preservation of rhinoceroses and one of the world's foremost authorities on the species."<ref name="EBEntry" /> Following Merz's death, a female rhinoceros calf born in April 2013 was named Anna after the conservationist.<ref name="APObit" /> A children's picture book by Daniel Kirk called ''Rhino In The House'' was published in early 2017 and features Merz and Samia.<ref name="KR2017">{{cite journal|title=Kirk, Daniel: Rhino in the House|url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/A479234657/GPS?u=wikipedia&sid=GPS&xid=4c909ff0|journal=[[Kirkus Reviews]]|date=1 February 2017|accessdate=22 December 2020|via=Gale General OneFile|url-access=subscription|archive-date=22 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204706/https://go.gale.com/ps/i.do?p=GPS&u=wikipedia&id=GALE%7CA479234657&v=2.1&it=r&sid=GPS&asid=4c909ff0|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hunter|first=Sarah|date=1 March 2017|title=Rhino in the House: The True Story of Saving Sarnia|url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/A488689571/GPS?u=wikipedia&sid=GPS&xid=2250a956|journal=[[Booklist]]|volume=113|issue=13|pages=58|url-access=subscription|access-date=22 December 2020|via=Gale In Context: Biography|archive-date=22 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204708/https://go.gale.com/ps/i.do?p=GPS&u=wikipedia&id=GALE%7CA488689571&v=2.1&it=r&sid=GPS&asid=2250a956|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2019, an illustrated fictional book detailing how Merz rescued and looked after Samia in the rhinoceros' formative years called ''Anna & Samia: The True Story of Saving a Black Rhino'' was written by Paul Meisel.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ford|first=Danielle J.|date=12 February 2020|title=Review of Anna & Samia: The True Story of Saving a Black Rhino|url=https://www.hbook.com/?detailStory=review-of-anna-and-samia-the-true-story-of-saving-a-black-rhino|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222204707/https://www.hbook.com/?detailStory=review-of-anna-and-samia-the-true-story-of-saving-a-black-rhino|archive-date=22 December 2020|access-date=22 December 2020|website=[[The Horn Book Magazine]]}}</ref>
